name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married into Hillcrest, my husband Adam's family farm, sixteen years ago. We keep about 250 dairy goats, grow hay and oats, and I make cheese with my mother-in-law Halima in the old stone dairy. My mornings are milking, then the cheese room, then labels, orders and the market stall on Saturdays. Adam does the fields and the machinery with his father Ismail. We live in our own house at the top of the lane, which is where the mortgage comes in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Doing three jobs at once, mother, farmer, cheesemaker. Hana's thirteen and Bilal's ten, and they both help at kidding time, which I love. I'll use an AI tool now and then to write a cheese description or a post for the stall, but Halima doesn't trust it. She says if a machine can describe the cheese, it should try making it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. It's what I'd expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy little helper for the paperwork and that's all. Good cheese still needs good hands, and no computer is going to change that. I'd say that at the stall if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. Our cheese sells because it's made by a family, by hand, and that wouldn't change. The worries stay the same, feed costs, the vet bill and whether the Saturday market keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are. I'd use the AI a bit more for the stall's posts and maybe the bookkeeping. We'd keep putting 150 a month aside and maybe buy a second cheese vat next year, about 4,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Halima make of the AI writing your cheese descriptions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She read one out loud at dinner in a funny posh voice and the kids laughed for ten minutes. Then she said the words my mother-in-law always says: the description was fine, but the machine forgot to mention the thyme. She was right, it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here you'd want to change on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe a better milking system for the goats, once a few other goat farms have one. We're not the kind to be first.

S0.say: It's a handy little helper for the paperwork and that's all. Good cheese still needs good hands, and no computer is going to change that.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because our cheese sells for being made by hand by a family. The worries stay feed costs, the vet bill and whether the Saturday market keeps going.
S0.do: Keeps going as the family always has and uses AI a little more for posts and bookkeeping. Keeps saving 150 a month and considers a second cheese vat for about 4,000.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: My mother-in-law said the description was fine, but the machine forgot to mention the thyme.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's identity is bound up with handmade family cheese. She uses AI lightly and only for words, never the craft. Her mother-in-law's scepticism is affectionate and shapes the household's attitude.

steps.text: Keep making Hillcrest goat cheese by hand with Halima and run the Saturday stall
Use the AI a bit more for the stall's posts and the bookkeeping
Keep putting 150 a month aside towards a 4,000 second cheese vat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's closer to what Adam reads about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families who work hard and look after each other will be fine. You change what you need to and keep what matters. I'd say that to friends at the mosque and to the other stallholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit about cheap cheese. If big dairies get robots that make decent goat cheese for half our cost, the people who just want a cheap cheese stop coming to the stall. We'd keep the customers who care, but there might be fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see how the robot milking systems do on two or three goat farms before we touch one. We'd save a bit more, 200 a month, and hold off on the second vat. I'd try selling to two restaurants in town, so we're not just relying on the stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry that sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Adam and Ismail say about robot milking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adam would want it tomorrow, he loves machines. Ismail would say his father milked by hand and so did he. I'd be in the middle, as usual, and probably the one who decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help farms like yours, if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the community. I don't want the government paying us to make cheese. If we can't sell it, we should make something people will buy.

S1.say: Families who work hard and look after each other will be fine. You change what you need to and keep what matters.
S1.think: I'd worry about cheap cheese: if big dairies get robots that make decent goat cheese for half our cost, the bargain hunters stop coming to the stall. We'd keep the customers who care, but fewer of them.
S1.do: Waits to see robot milking working on two or three goat farms before considering one. Raises savings to 200 a month, holds off the second vat and tries selling to two restaurants in town.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a small worry that stays put.
S1.quote: I don't want the government paying us to make cheese. If we can't sell it, we should make something people will buy.
S1.fieldNote: Sara sits between her husband's love of machines and her father-in-law's tradition, and is likely the decider. She looks for new customers rather than outside help. Her worry is cheaper competition, not losing her own work.

steps.text: Wait until robot milkers work on two or three goat farms first
Raise savings to 200 a month and hold off on the second vat
Start selling Hillcrest cheese to two restaurants in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office work in two years, and the hands three years after. Our cheese is all hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the stall I'd say handmade cheese is safe for a good while yet, because no machine can do our work until 2031. I'd tell the other stallholders to look after their regulars. At the mosque I'd say families have to hold together, because a lot of people would lose their jobs in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't worry about the goats or the dairy first, I worry about who buys from us. Half our Saturday regulars work in offices in town, the bank, the council, the insurance place. If their wages go in 2028, a 9 wedge of cheese is the first thing that comes off the list, three years before any robot touches our milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the second vat and the holiday, and put the 150 a month on the mortgage instead. I'd let the AI take over the labels, the orders and the books properly, because by then everyone would be using it. And I'd take a stall at a second market in the next town, so we're not leaning on one set of customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the farm, which Adam's parents own outright, but for our own house at the top of the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which regulars are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a man from the council planning office who buys the same thyme cheese every Saturday and tells me about his grandchildren. He's exactly the kind of person who'd lose his job in 2028. I'd keep his wedge aside even if he could only pay later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about selling the cheese more cheaply to keep customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd make a smaller wedge rather than a cheaper cheese. You don't give up your place at the market for a quick sale. Halima spent twenty years earning our pitch at the Saturday market, and I won't throw it away in one bad year.

S2.say: Handmade cheese is safe for a good while yet, because no machine can do our work until 2031. Families have to hold together, because a lot of people will lose their jobs in 2028.
S2.think: I worry less about the goats than about who buys from us. Half our Saturday regulars work in offices in town, and if their wages go in 2028, cheese is the first thing off the list, three years before any robot touches our milking.
S2.do: Stops the second vat and the holiday and puts the 150 a month on the house mortgage. Hands labels, orders and books fully to the AI and takes a stall at a second market in the next town.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for the farm, which her in-laws own outright, but for the family's own house.
S2.quote: Halima spent twenty years earning our pitch at the Saturday market, and I won't throw it away in one bad year.
S2.fieldNote: Sara spotted that the 2028 thinking AI hits her office-worker customers long before robots reach her cheese room. Her response is to protect the market pitch and spread her customers, not to compete on price. The in-laws owning the farm outright is what keeps this from being worse for her.

steps.text: Drop the second cheese vat and the holiday; put 150 a month on the mortgage
Hand Hillcrest's labels, orders and books fully to the AI
Take a cheese stall at a second market in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking, eight for the robots. That's time to watch other people go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families who plan ahead will be fine, and five years is time to plan. I'd say it to friends at the mosque and to the stallholders. You change what you need to and keep what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the cheese buyers are still my worry, but five years gives our regulars time to find new work. By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be 51 and Hana would be grown. If a robot milker has been proven on other goat farms by then, we'd have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving 200 a month and I'd start selling cheese online, with the AI writing the descriptions and Halima checking them. In year three, if two or three goat farms have a robot milker working well, we'd put about 10,000 into one. And I'd make sure Hana takes her exams seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can plan, and planning calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ismail say about the robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no for a year and then stand watching it for an hour on the first day. I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one. Ismail is the same, he just says it louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want for Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana wants to be a pharmacist. I'd tell my daughter to go for it, and come home at kidding time like she always has.

S3.say: Families who plan ahead will be fine, and five years is time to plan. You change what you need to and keep what matters.
S3.think: The cheese buyers are still my worry, but five years gives them time to find new work. By 2034 I'd be 51, Hana would be grown, and if robot milkers are proven on other goat farms, we'd have one.
S3.do: Keeps saving 200 a month and starts selling cheese online, with the AI writing descriptions and Halima checking them. Puts about 10,000 into a robot milker in year three if it's proven on other goat farms, and makes sure Hana takes her exams seriously.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but able to plan, and planning calms her.
S3.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one.
S3.fieldNote: Sara's steady approach fits this timeline well: watch others try it, then buy. She'd use the extra time to build online sales so the stall isn't the only outlet. The family's mix of generations shapes every choice.

steps.text: Start selling Hillcrest cheese online, with Halima checking the AI's descriptions
Buy a robot goat milker for about 10,000 in year three if proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for the robots. Bilal would be twenty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no need to rush. We'd see how it goes on other farms first, like we always do. People will still want cheese made by a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel fine. Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for the robots is a long time for a small farm, and our customers have time to adjust. By 2039 I'd be 56 and Halima would probably have stopped making cheese, so the cheese room would be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for two or three years, then buy a proven robot milker for about 8,000. I'd build up online cheese sales slowly. And I'd start funds of 50 a month for Hana and Bilal's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels far enough away to plan without worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the mornings change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a robot milker I'd lose the quiet half hour at six with the goats, which I'd miss. That half hour is my time to think. I'd probably still go in and stand with them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hillcrest still be a family farm in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so. Bilal loves the goats more than Hana does, so maybe him. A family farm with a robot milker is still a family farm.

S4.say: There's no need to rush. We'd see how it goes on other farms first, like we always do, because people will still want cheese made by a family.
S4.think: Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for the robots is a long time for a small farm. By 2039 I'd be 56 and the cheese room would probably be mine, with Halima retired.
S4.do: Watches for two or three years, then buys a proven robot milker for about 8,000. Builds online cheese sales slowly and starts funds of 50 a month for Hana and Bilal's training.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels far enough away to plan without worrying.
S4.quote: A family farm with a robot milker is still a family farm.
S4.fieldNote: With a long timeline Sara is relaxed and plans the handover within the family. She would take a robot milker once proven, even though it costs her the quiet morning half hour she loves. Her son, not her daughter, is the one she sees carrying the farm on.

steps.text: Watch other goat farms for two or three years before buying anything
Buy a proven robot goat milker for about 8,000
Start funds of 50 a month for Hana and Bilal's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our customers in the offices would lose their wages in two years, before we'd had time to find new ones. What would help is time and family, and maybe help to sell our cheese further away, but not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats themselves. People think farming is about money, but some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is. A robot doesn't feel that.

headlineQuote: Some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is.
portrait: Sara Ibrahim, 43, married into Hillcrest, her husband's family goat farm, where she makes handmade cheese with her mother-in-law and runs a Saturday market stall. She uses AI now and then for labels and posts, trusts family and faith over government and waits for others to prove new machines. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about cheap robot cheese under steady change. Fast AGI makes her anxious, not for the cheese room, which robots can't touch until 2031, but because her office-worker customers would lose their wages in 2028, so she'd cut back and add a second market. With more time she'd adopt proven robot milkers and sell cheese online.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her office-worker customers would lose their wages before she could find new ones.
whatWouldHelp: Time, family, and help selling cheese further afield, but not handouts.
